Throughout the Great Depression, a watchful bird kept its single ghastly eye permanently open as my grandfather spent every evening for an entire year roaming his cornfields. He understood existence as an endless succession of pigs confined in an endless succession of pens. The bird consequently overheard him wondering whether he ought to use his finest firearm, a machete, his Buick, or a rope to free himself from the tedious cycle of breakfast, lunch, dinner, sunrise, sunset, autumn, winter, spring, summer, and all the rest.

Yet his daughters were beautiful and baked excellent pies, so he continued his miserable life beneath the bird’s gaze. Cancer eventually killed him by more natural means, before he could witness his family turn into the drug users, physician-haters, masturbators, insomniacs, compulsive sleepers, recluses, and abstainers from alcohol that the bird had foreseen. After all, girls exist merely to spoil everything through reckless reproduction, until now, now, now the onslaught has truly become unceasing: his descendants’ limbs grew so burdensome, and the raging wind therefore became so overwhelming.

Behind the bird’s eye, however, rests its tiny gray brain; beneath that lies a heart—I swear—and through that heart pass the uncertain notes of this merciless song.

During the Great Depression, a vigilant one-eyed bird watched from the edge of the cornfields as the narrator’s grandfather wandered among the rows each evening. For an entire year, he followed the same paths, burdened by the sense that existence had become repetitive, exhausting, and without purpose. In his despair, he often contemplated ending his life.

What kept him alive was his love for his daughters and the small comforts they brought him, especially the pies they baked. These ordinary expressions of affection gave him enough reason to endure, even when his misery seemed overwhelming. He continued living until cancer eventually claimed him.

His death spared him from witnessing the struggles of later generations. His descendants developed their own addictions, aversions, compulsions, and habits of isolation, each finding a different way to bear or escape life’s pain. Meanwhile, the one-eyed bird remains a silent observer of this recurring cycle of suffering, survival, and reproduction. Within it are the uncertain notes of a cruel song—a song that may express grief, fate, or the bleak persistence of life itself.
outputs.L4:
The one-eyed bird watched from the fence post as the old man crossed the yard.

It had been there all winter, a ragged black shape against the white fields, its remaining eye bright and unblinking. Each morning the grandfather noticed it waiting in the same place. He sometimes wondered whether it was injured, stupid, or simply more patient than other creatures. Nothing seemed to frighten it away—not the wind, not the empty crack of the barn door, not even the distant engines of trucks carrying away the farms of men who could no longer pay for them.

The Depression had reduced his life to repetition. He rose before dawn, coaxed heat from damp wood, divided the last food into portions, and went outside to perform work that no longer promised improvement. The soil yielded less each year. Bills accumulated. Tools broke. His hands split and bled, healed, and split again. Every day seemed to be a copy of the one before it, only poorer.

That morning, he carried a length of rope into the barn.

The bird tilted its head as it watched him disappear through the doorway.

Inside, the old man stood beneath a beam and listened to the house settling in the cold. He imagined how quiet it would be when he was no longer required to answer hunger, debt, weather, or shame. He imagined the relief of stepping outside the machinery of living—the endless cycle of waking, laboring, worrying, and sleeping only to begin again.

Then he heard his daughters in the house.

One coughed in her sleep. The other murmured something he could not understand. Their voices reached him faintly, but they were enough. He saw them waking to find the barn still and their father absent from the breakfast table. He saw the question they would carry for the rest of their lives: whether they had not been sufficient reason for him to stay.

He lowered the rope.

This was called love, though it did not feel tender in that moment. It felt like a chain fastened around his ribs. Love did not rescue him from despair. It merely made escape impossible.

He returned to the house, prepared breakfast, and lived.

Years passed. His daughters grew, married, and had children of their own. The old man’s decision in the barn became invisible, buried beneath ordinary days. No one celebrated the mornings he endured. No one knew how often he had resented them. His continued existence was treated as natural, though it had required a choice he was forced to make again and again.

The children born from that choice inherited more than his name. They inherited his silences, his fear of poverty, his habit of confusing suffering with virtue. Some drank. Some disappeared into bad marriages. Some struck the people they loved and apologized afterward. Some learned to smile while imagining death. They produced children in turn, passing along their grief in altered forms: anxiety became discipline, loneliness became anger, devotion became control.

There were moments of happiness, certainly. Babies laughed. Families gathered around tables. Hands were held in hospital rooms. People forgave one another, briefly and imperfectly. Yet every tenderness carried a demand: remain alive, continue the line, bear what must be borne so that someone else will not be abandoned.

The grandfather lived long enough to see grandchildren and great-grandchildren. They called his endurance admirable. They praised the strength that had carried the family through hard times. None of them could see the barn as he still saw it, or the rope in his hands, or the one-eyed bird waiting outside.

The bird itself vanished years before. Perhaps it died in the field. Perhaps another animal took it. Perhaps, despite its ruined sight, it simply flew elsewhere. But in the grandfather’s memory it remained on the fence post, watching without judgment as one exhausted creature chose not to die.

That choice became a family.

The family became generations.

And the generations continued—loving, injuring, reproducing, surviving—each person fastening the next to life through need and affection. What began as mercy became obligation; what looked like courage became inheritance. Still they endured, not because existence had grown kinder, but because love kept making departure crueler than staying.
outputs.L5:
### Living With the Great Depression

The Great Depression was one of the most severe economic crises in modern history. Beginning in 1929, it caused widespread unemployment, poverty, and financial instability around the world. Many families struggled to survive, with limited access to food, housing, and basic necessities.

Governments responded with new economic policies and public programs designed to create jobs and restore confidence. In the United States, President Franklin D. Roosevelt introduced the New Deal, which provided relief to millions of people and reformed the financial system.

Living with the Great Depression demanded resilience, cooperation, and sacrifice. Although recovery took many years, the experience influenced economic policy and changed how governments respond to financial crises.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a single-paragraph Southern Gothic prose poem about a grandfather contemplating suicide during the Great Depression while an ominous one-eyed bird watches his family’s future unravel.
counterfactuals.output: In the summer the banks died, Granddaddy sat beneath the lightning-struck pecan with his father’s pistol cooling like a black fish in his lap, while dust sifted through the cotton rows and Mama boiled stones to keep the children believing in supper. On the fencepost, a one-eyed crow watched him with its good eye bright as judgment, cocking its head toward all that had not happened yet: the eldest boy vanishing into the mills, the baby girl marrying a man with thunder in his hands, the farmhouse sinking porch-first into trumpet vine, every family photograph paling until their faces looked drowned. Granddaddy listened to the empty barn creak its old hymns and wondered whether death was a door or only another room the poor were made to sweep. The pistol grew heavier; the crow grew still. Somewhere beyond the ruined fields, his unborn grandson began already to dream of fire, and the whole bloodline trembled like a loose thread caught in the bird’s beak, waiting to be pulled.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental, darkly comic family history narrated through the perspective of a vigilant bird, blending rural hardship, existential despair, generational decline, and grotesque imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
### The Rook Keeps the Records

I have watched the Bellweather family for six generations, which is longer than any sensible creature would watch anything except a field mouse.

They built their house beneath my ash tree in 1871, though *built* is generous. They persuaded several boards to lean against one another and filled the arguments between them with mud. The first winter, snow came through the roof and settled on the children’s blankets. Ezekiel Bellweather called this “ventilation.” His wife, Mercy, called it nothing. She had lost three teeth, two infants, and the habit of complaint.

I was there.

A rook remembers what people bury.

Ezekiel arrived with one mule, one Bible, and a jar containing a pickled human thumb. He claimed the thumb belonged to a saint. Mercy said it belonged to his brother Amos, who had misplaced it in a threshing machine.

Either way, it brought no luck.

Their farm was fourteen acres of clay, stones, and theological disappointment. Corn emerged reluctantly. Potatoes developed personalities and hid. The mule, Episcopalian by temperament, refused labor on feast days no one else recognized.

Every evening, Ezekiel stood at the fence and surveyed his kingdom.

“Next year,” he said.

This became the family motto.

NEXT YEAR.

They never carved it over the door because they could not afford a door.

***

Their eldest son, Hiram, inherited the farm and the thumb.

He married a woman named Temperance because rural families in those days named daughters after qualities they hoped misfortune might beat into them. Temperance was neither temperate nor patient. She could drink lamp oil without blinking and once broke a preacher’s jaw with a frozen turnip.

I admired her.

Under Hiram, the farm declined from hopeless to allegorical. The west field flooded every spring, though it stood on a hill. The cows gave milk that smelled faintly of pennies. A lightning strike killed the scarecrow but spared the crows, which Hiram considered a personal insult.

It was not personal.

We disliked the scarecrow.

Hiram and Temperance produced eight children, of whom five survived infancy, four survived childhood, and three survived one another. At supper they sat around a table made from Ezekiel’s coffin lid. Ezekiel himself had been buried in a flour crate after Mercy decided practicality was next to godliness.

At night, the children listened to rats inside the walls.

“Are they eating the house?” little Patience asked.

“No,” said Temperance. “They’re eating what holds it up.”

This comforted no one, but it was accurate.

***

The third generation discovered machinery.

Silas Bellweather purchased a steam thresher on credit from a man with waxed mustaches and the ethics of a tapeworm. The machine was red, magnificent, and hungry. It coughed black smoke over the fields and devoured grain, gloves, a pitchfork, half a Sunday coat, and eventually Silas’s left arm.

The arm was buried beside Amos’s thumb, though not before Silas accused it of abandoning him.

After the accident he wore an empty sleeve pinned to his shoulder. In winter, starlings nested in it.

I objected to this. A sleeve is not a proper nest. It lacks drainage.

Silas’s wife, Abigail, took over the work. She plowed, sowed, harvested, butchered, bartered, delivered calves and babies, and dug the grave when Silas finally drowned in six inches of cider.

The family called it a tragedy.

Abigail called it Tuesday.

Her children grew long and pale, with the strained look of vegetables raised in cellars. One became a schoolteacher and fled west. One joined the army and returned convinced he was a church bell. At noon he stood in the yard and shouted *BONG* until the neighbors adjusted their clocks.

The youngest, Ruth, stayed.

Someone always stays.

That is how ruins reproduce.

***

Ruth married her cousin Edwin, narrowing both the bloodline and the conversation.

By then the house had developed a permanent tilt toward the family graveyard, as if eager to join it. Edwin repaired nothing. He believed decay was God’s bookkeeping.

“Everything goes back to dust,” he said.

“Not the mortgage,” Ruth replied.

They had one son, Vernon, who was born with a caul over his face and spent the rest of his life behaving as if it remained there. He feared wells, mirrors, geese, buttons, weather, and the possibility that other people were real. He slept beneath the kitchen table until he was thirty-two.

Vernon inherited the farm during the Great Drying, when the creek became a scar and the cattle stood in the pasture with their ribs showing like the bars of small prisons. Dust entered the bread, the beds, the lungs. It coated the dead in their graves, though they had no use for cleanliness.

I watched the Bellweathers eat crow once.

Not me.

A cousin.

We have not forgotten.

Vernon apologized before every bite, which my cousin would have found insufficient.

***

Then came electricity.

A wire arrived at the house like a black vine from the future. Vernon’s son Earl touched it with a wet hand and spent the next hour speaking fluent Latin, despite never having attended school past the age of nine. Unfortunately, all he said was:

*Where am I? Where am I? Where am I?*

An excellent question, wasted on the electrocuted.

Earl married June, who had beautiful red hair and a laugh like plates breaking. She wanted to leave the farm. She packed a suitcase every birthday. Each year something stopped her: a sick child, a dead cow, a bad harvest, a good harvest, Earl’s lungs, Earl’s temper, Earl’s apologies, the price of gasoline, the weather, inertia—that most faithful member of any family.

Her suitcase remained beside the bed for forty-three years.

When she died, they opened it.

Inside were a blue dress, a train timetable, twenty-seven dollars, and the skeleton of a mouse curled in one shoe.

Even I found that excessive.

***

Earl’s children sold the north field, then the south field, then the woods. They sold the tractor, the silver, the mineral rights, Mercy’s wedding ring, and the saintly thumb, which fetched twelve dollars at a roadside curiosity shop.

Thus does a relic become lunch.

Only Len remained, the last Bellweather, though he had a daughter somewhere in Ohio who sent Christmas cards depicting smiling people in matching sweaters. Len pinned them to the wall without opening them.

He lived in three rooms of the collapsing house. Chickens occupied the others. One winter, a sow wandered into the parlor and gave birth beneath a portrait of Hiram. The piglets ate the frame. Hiram’s painted face fell forward and lay among them, dignified at last by manure.

Len laughed for ten minutes.

Then he cried until morning.

Humans often confuse these noises.

***

Last March, the roof surrendered.

It did not collapse dramatically. It sighed inward during a rainstorm, like an old woman lowering herself into a bath. Len was sitting at the coffin-lid table, eating beans from the pot. A rafter pinned his coat but missed his body.

For three hours he believed himself trapped.

Then the coat tore.

He stood in the rain among broken beams, wet plaster, feathers, photographs, mouse nests, pig bones, unpaid bills, and the accumulated objects by which a family proves it happened.

He looked up at me.

“You’ve seen it all,” he said.

I had.

“Was there any point?”

This is the sort of question humans ask birds because they cannot bear the answers of other humans.

I considered Ezekiel and his ventilation. Mercy’s silence. Temperance’s turnip. Silas’s abandoned arm. June’s packed suitcase. Six generations planting into bad soil because next year might be less cruel, because hunger is repetitive, because hope is often only despair with its sleeves rolled up.

I cleaned my beak against the branch.

Then I flew down and stole a bean from his pot.

Len began laughing again.

Above us, the ash tree—my ash tree, older than the house and wiser than the family—split along its rotten heart.

One half fell toward the graveyard.

The other fell toward the road.

I chose the road.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a long, breathless sentence about an old farmer wandering his cornfields, considering ways to end his life, but choosing to survive because of his daughters and their pies; conclude with the bird observing his descendants’ dysfunction.
counterfactuals.output: The old farmer wandered his cornfields beneath a sky the color of worn tin, brushing the dry leaves with his knotted hands and turning over, as relentlessly as the crows turned above him, all the ways a man might quietly step out of his own life and leave the wind to erase his footprints, yet whenever he neared that dark decision he saw his daughters at the kitchen table with flour on their cheeks and anger, laughter, and stubborn love in their voices, setting down apple pies still breathing cinnamon into the room, and he understood that grief could wait, that death could wait, that he would go home and eat one more warm slice with them, then another through all the difficult years granted him, while from the fence post a blackbird watched the generations gather afterward, multiplying old wounds into new quarrels, marriages, estrangements, and ruined holidays, calmly observing his descendants’ dysfunction.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal literary monologue featuring the repeated words “one,” “bird,” and “now,” with run-on lists, cyclical references to meals and seasons, and a final image of a cruel song passing through the bird’s heart.
counterfactuals.output:
One morning, or one winter pretending to be morning, I found a bird asleep in the blue bowl where yesterday’s soup had cooled into a small gray moon, and I said one, because there was one bird, one bowl, one window trembling with frost, though now I remember two wings, three shadows, four crumbs arranged like a calendar no one had finished reading.

Bird, I whispered, bird, bird.

Now the kettle began its metallic weather. Now the spoons stirred themselves. Now breakfast became supper became breakfast again: bread and salt and pear skins, broth and blackberries, eggshells, cloves, a fish with a silver eye, a cake collapsed beneath the weight of its candles, and outside spring opened its green mouth, summer poured bees into it, autumn filled the bees with smoke, winter returned the bowl to the table and the table to the room and the room to the one morning where the bird still slept.

I was hungry then. I am hungry now. I will be hungry when the orchard climbs through the floorboards and hangs its bitter fruit from the ceiling, when the chairs kneel, when the clock lays one white egg after another and each egg hatches the same hour.

One hour.

One bird.

Now.

At noon I served the bird a feast of impossible things: the first snow of August, the last apple of spring, a cup of thunder, a ribbon cut from my mother’s voice, lentils, lilies, ash, seven red seeds, one red seed, no seed at all, and the bird ate everything except hunger. Hunger it left for me.

So I swallowed the winter. I swallowed the supper. I swallowed the little blue bowl and found inside it the morning, and inside the morning the bird, and inside the bird one room with one table where I sat eating breakfast, supper, breakfast, while spring became summer became autumn became winter became spring, and now was then, and then was now, and one was never one for long.

Bird, I said, what season is the heart?

The bird opened its eyes.

From far away—or from the bowl, or the clock, or the orchard growing upside down inside my chest—came a music sharp as a knife laid beside the bread. It entered the room without opening the door. It circled once around the table, once around the year, once around my name.

Then the cruel song passed through the bird’s heart.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a bleak, lyrical piece of flash fiction set partly during the Great Depression, exploring suicide, cancer, reproduction, inherited misery, and the relentless passage of time through bizarre rural symbolism.
counterfactuals.output:
In 1933, the year the bank took the west field, Ada Wren found a pocket watch growing inside a turnip.

Its pale roots had threaded through the brass. The hands still moved, though backward, ticking toward some hour already spent. Ada carried it home in her apron and set it beside her father’s bowl.

“What’s it count?” he asked.

“Us,” she said.

Her father had been coughing blood into seed catalogs. There was no money for a doctor, only mustard plasters and the preacher’s white knuckles. Cancer was a word town people used; in the country they called it a bad place, as if the body were acreage and death a tenant who would not leave.

That winter, Ada married Silas Vale because his family owned three milk cows and because hunger, like love, makes promises with the mouth.

Silas had inherited a sorrow so old nobody remembered its first owner. His grandfather had walked into the river with stones in his coat. His mother had hanged blue jars from every fence post to trap the ghosts, but the ghosts went into her children instead. Silas carried his quietly. It slept beside him, ate from his plate, put its cold feet against Ada’s in bed.

Their first baby was born without breath during a dust storm. Their second lived long enough to open her eyes. In each pupil, Ada thought she saw the backward watch.

Afterward the hens began laying black eggs. When cracked, they held no yolk, only small wet feathers. The preacher said famine produced oddities. Ada said nothing. She buried the eggs beneath the pear tree, and in spring the tree bloomed with tiny white teeth.

Years passed by hiding themselves in chores.

Silas repaired fences. Ada bled, conceived, miscarried. The cows calved. The calves became cows. The west field went from bank to railway to a man in Chicago who never saw it. Each autumn, thousands of starlings rose from the corn in the shape of a woman falling.

One June morning, Silas left his boots neatly beneath the sycamore and walked into the river, as his grandfather had. The water was shallow, but grief requires little depth.

They found him downstream among the reeds, his shirt full of minnows.

Ada did not forgive him. This was how she kept him alive.

She raised their surviving son, Thomas, on milk, bitterness, and stories pared down to the bone. She never told him about the stones in the grandfather’s coat. She never told him sorrow could be hereditary. Still, as a boy, Thomas woke some nights with river mud between his toes.

Then came war, then highways, then television, then men on the moon. Time, having starved during the Depression, grew fat and impatient. It ate the barn. It ate the pear tree. It ate Ada’s teeth and memory. On her ninety-first birthday, she looked at Thomas and asked why there was a river in his face.

By then, something had begun flowering in his lungs.

The doctor showed him the gray blossoms on a screen. “Cancer,” she said, giving the old bad place its modern name.

Thomas had two daughters, and both had children of their own. Fertility had returned to the family like rain to a graveyard. Babies bloomed everywhere—pink, furious, innocent—each one gripping the air as though trying to stop the invisible machinery.

At the hospital, Thomas gave his eldest daughter the turnip watch. The brass was green now, the roots long dried to threads.

“It runs backward,” she said.

“No,” he told her. “We do.”

That night he dreamed of Ada standing in the stolen west field. She was young and pregnant, though the child inside her was also Ada, and inside that Ada another child slept, and inside that child another, mothers nested through the dark like coffins.

Behind them stood Silas, dripping river water. Behind Silas stood his grandfather. Behind the grandfather stood a black animal with a clock for a head, chewing the stars one by one.

Thomas woke before dawn. For a moment, he considered the window, the height, the clean conclusion of gravity. Then his newborn grandson began crying in the next room.

The sound was terrible. The sound was ordinary. It passed through the walls like a nail driven through generations.

Thomas lay back and listened.

Outside, beneath the hospital’s electric glare, a farmerless tractor crossed a field that had once belonged to someone. In its wake, the earth turned up watches, teeth, blue glass, black eggs, wedding rings, and the small blind skulls of mice.

Morning came without mercy.

It always had.
